title: The Cost of a Free Cup
subtitle: A Lanternweald continuation
content:
I knew the pantry had a problem when Iroh began measuring tea leaves with the precision of a military engineer.

Normally, he measured by smell. He would lift a tin, breathe in, and make a thoughtful little sound that told me whether he approved of the harvest. That morning, every scoop went onto the scale.

"Have you developed a sudden love of arithmetic?" I asked.

"Arithmetic has never wounded my pride by insisting I steep mountain mint in boiling water."

"That was one time."

"An educational catastrophe."

He balanced the scale and wrote a number in the margin of his ledger.

Outside the Jasmine Steps storefront, rain slipped from tiled roofs into the gutter. A handful of children raced toward Lanternwell Square with loaves wrapped under their coats. The public notice board carried a fresh announcement about the coming Longlight meal.

FREE TEA FOR ALL VISITORS, someone had written at the bottom.

I suspected the handwriting belonged to Maui.

"How many visitors?" I asked.

Iroh pointed at the last entry. "Thirty-four yesterday. Forty-two the day before. The pantry has been open a month, and I have yet to see a proper record of what comes out."

"People need tea."

"Of course. But the leaves do not grow faster because I wish them to."

I leaned against the counter and watched his hands.

He was not angry that people were drinking what he offered. He was angry because he had offered something he could not sustain and could not bear to take back. I recognized that flaw. It had lived in me long enough to pay rent.

"Come to the square with me," I said.

"I have a shop to open."

"We have an hour."

He raised an eyebrow.

"That is enough time to accomplish very little efficiently."

"Perfect. My specialty."

At the square, the bakery door stood open. Mara was stacking bread behind a counter, muttering at a shelf that refused to sit level. A young courier named Pip had three baskets at their feet and a list so long it touched the floor.

Neri stood beside the well, reading a complaint.

"Tea has become too expensive for the west-side households," they told us.

Iroh's shoulders settled into an expression I had seen before, the one he wore when someone else's need turned into an obligation he could imagine meeting only by doing more himself.

"We can continue serving without charge," he began.

"With what?" I asked.

He looked at me.

"The same kettle we've used all week?"

"With a revised blend."

"Made from which leaves?"

Mara did not look up from the bread.

"Oh, good. Somebody finally asked."

That was how I learned the pantry ledger had three separate sets of numbers and no shared understanding of what counted as a donation. One person recorded sacks of flour. Another counted loaves after baking. A third had entered the same flour twice because they thought everything arriving at the bakery belonged to the pantry.

Pip looked close to tears.

"I thought I was helping."

"You were," I said. "The records are confusing. That's a problem with the system, not proof you failed."

Iroh set his tea tin on the table.

"Perhaps I have contributed to the confusion," he admitted.

Mara finally raised her head. "You, old man? Never."

"I have been giving away tea from my private stores without making a record of it."

"And telling the children it is free forever," she said.

I winced.

Iroh looked as though someone had criticized the quality of his heart.

"I meant to be kind."

"I know." Mara wiped flour from her hands. "But if you run out, the children won't get tea tomorrow. If you tell them what the kitchen has, they can help decide how to stretch it."

We spent the morning in an argument so ordinary it felt almost luxurious. Nobody was being chased. No army waited beyond the wall. The problem could be written in columns.

I made three headings: SUPPLIED, USED, NEEDED.

Pip measured the remaining flour and nearly sneezed into the bag. Mara counted loaves. Iroh opened every tea tin, including the one he had been hiding beneath the counter because its leaves were too expensive to use freely.

"That tin has a name," I said.

"It is a special harvest."

"Is its name 'I'm saving this for an imaginary emergency'?"

He gave me a look.

"It is old," he said.

"That was not an answer."

He hesitated, then touched the metal lid.

"Lu Ten liked this blend."

My pen stopped.

The square's sounds went on without waiting for us. A cart rattled over the stones. Someone laughed in the bakery. Neri spoke softly to a traveler near the arches.

Iroh had not looked at me when he said his son's name. He was looking at the tin, seeing another table, another time.

"We don't have to use it," I told him.

"I know."

"I mean it. The pantry is not entitled to everything you own just because you know how to help."

He breathed out. "I have been telling myself I was keeping it for an occasion worthy of him. Then each occasion passed."

"Maybe you can keep it. Maybe you can brew some for yourself. You get to decide."

His gaze found mine.

"You have become quite demanding about choice."

"I learned from an irritatingly good teacher."

"Who might that be?"

"Don't make me say it. His ego is fragile."

The corner of his mouth moved.

We agreed on a plan by noon. Free tea would remain available, but the sign would say while supplies lasted. People who could contribute leaves, water, cups or time could do so without being given moral superiority over those who could not. The pantry would keep one ledger, visible to anyone who wanted to check it. And Iroh would teach three volunteers to make a balanced inexpensive blend so the work did not depend on his presence.

Maui appeared while I was replacing the sign.

"Why did my announcement change?"

"Because promises need supplies," I said.

"I promised tea."

"Yes. That was the problem."

He considered this for a dramatic three seconds, then offered to carry water from the spring.

"Good," I said. "Ask Neri where it can be taken from first."

He opened his mouth, saw my expression, and went to ask.

Iroh watched him leave.

"A hero learning to fetch water," he mused. "There may yet be hope for the world."

When evening came, we closed the little tea counter and returned to Ba Sing Se. The Jasmine Dragon smelled of rain and warm ceramic. Iroh took the special tin from his satchel and set it between us.

"Will you have a cup?" he asked.

"Only if you want to make it."

"I do."

He prepared the tea slowly. Not because the leaves were precious, but because he no longer needed to hurry to justify keeping them.

The first sip was lighter than I expected, with a bright, almost citrus edge under the jasmine. Iroh watched me taste it.

"Well?"

"Lu Ten had good taste."

"He did."

I reached across the table and placed my hand beside his. He turned his palm upward, waiting.

I put my hand in it.

We sat that way for a while.

"I have enjoyed our home becoming larger," he said. "But I do not want the larger world to consume all the small things."

"Neither do I."

He traced the rim of my cup with his free hand. "You have other people to care for, other promises. I know we have spoken about them. I would be foolish to assume that means my wish for your company has become smaller."

"You can ask me to stay for tea."

"And if you are needed elsewhere?"

"I'll tell you. And we can choose another day."

He nodded.

"Then I would like tomorrow evening."

"You're requesting an appointment?"

"I am courting a very difficult person."

"That is rude."

"It is accurate."

I leaned across the table. His beard brushed my cheek as he kissed me, warm and unhurried. He still tasted faintly of jasmine, and I found myself smiling.

Somewhere behind us the kettle started to hiss.

"That," I said, "has terrible timing."

"On the contrary," Iroh murmured. "It has learned from us."

We finished the tea before it cooled. The tin remained on the table.

Not sacrificed. Not hidden.

Used, at last, because the person who owned it had chosen to share.
